analysis.one_liner: Bans firing or refusing to hire workers because of their sexual orientation or gender identity.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 45 Senate cosponsors, including two Republicans, and got one Senate hearing, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for employers with 15 or more employees, employment agencies, and labor unions to fire, refuse to hire, or otherwise discriminate against someone because of their actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity. It would be enforced the same way as existing federal race and sex discrimination law, with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission handling complaints and courts hearing suits, including suits against state and federal government employers. The bill carved out exemptions for religious organizations and the armed forces, allowed only intentional-discrimination claims, barred quotas, and defined marriage according to the Defense of Marriage Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender, and workers perceived as such, including federal, state, and local government employees. They would gain a federal legal cause of action, with the same procedures and remedies available under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, when an employer fires, refuses to hire, or mistreats them because of their sexual orientation or gender identity, and protection against retaliation for complaining.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered employers, employment agencies, and labor organizations from failing to hire, discharging, or otherwise discriminating against any individual because of actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity.
Gives the EEOC, the Attorney General, and federal courts the same enforcement powers, procedures, and remedies they already have under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Extends protection to government employment, allowing actions against the United States and the states and stripping states of 11th Amendment immunity for violations.
Prohibits retaliation against workers who oppose discrimination or participate in an investigation or hearing.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers with 15 or more employees, which would face the same complaint, investigation, and lawsuit exposure that already applies under federal race and sex discrimination law, plus posting requirements. Religious organizations and the armed forces are exempt, and no new facilities construction is required.

drawbacks.text: The bill adopts the Defense of Marriage Act definition of marriage and explicitly does not require employers to treat unmarried couples the same as married ones for benefits, so same-sex couples would gain anti-discrimination protection at work but not equal spousal benefits under this bill.
Religious organizations are exempt, leaving them free to make employment decisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Only intentional (disparate treatment) discrimination claims are allowed; workers could not bring claims based on policies that have a discriminatory effect without intent, and the EEOC is barred from collecting statistics on sexual orientation or gender identity, limiting enforcement data.

Employers would absorb litigation and compliance costs, and critics objected to expanded legal exposure and to the shared-facilities provisions, though the bill allows uniform dress, grooming, and facility rules and does not require new facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large for the workers covered: a federal right not to be fired for being or being perceived as gay or transgender, enforceable with familiar Title VII tools. The costs are deliberately contained — the 15-employee threshold, the religious exemption, the ban on quotas and disparate-impact claims, and the DOMA marriage definition all narrow both the protection and the burden on employers. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the protections were written conservatively, and that workers at religious organizations and same-sex couples seeking benefits parity were left out.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's labor committee held one hearing on the bill but never voted to advance it, and the Senate never brought it to the floor before the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 5, 2009 by Senator Jeff Merkley with 39 original cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
It accumulated 45 cosponsors, including 41 of 58 Senate Democrats, the chamber's independents, and two Republicans, Senators Collins and Snowe.
The committee held a hearing on November 5, 2009, which was the only action the bill received.
The bill was never reported out of committee and never received a Senate floor vote; the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 with the bill dead.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, which remained free to fire or refuse to hire workers for being or being perceived as gay or transgender without federal liability, and religious organizations, which kept full freedom in employment decisions. Workers in states without their own protection remained without recourse.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 44 cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and convened the committee's hearing on it in November 2009.

for.name: 41 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, along with the chamber's two independents.

for.name: Susan Collins and Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the few employment bills of the period with Republican Senate support.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote during the two years the Democratic-led chamber had it.

against.name: 38 of 40 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate Republicans who did not cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Did not cosponsor the bill; only two Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached the floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 41 of 58 Democrats plus both independents signed on, versus 2 of 40 Republicans — though the two Republican cosponsors gave it formal bipartisan sponsorship, and no vote ever split the chamber.

industries.industry: Private and government employers with 15 or more employees
industries.note: The bill would have subjected them to EEOC enforcement and lawsuits for firing or refusing to hire based on sexual orientation or gender identity, the same regime already applying to race and sex discrimination. Their interest in avoiding that liability runs against workers' interest in protection.

The bill explicitly exempts religious organizations covered by the Civil Rights Act's religious-employer provisions, preserving their ability to make employment decisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
Also covered entities under the bill, liable for discriminatory referral, membership, or apprenticeship practices.
